cur.name: Current IRI
cur.tagline: Scales every indicator between this quarter's best and worst country.
cur.how: Each quarter, extreme values are clipped, then every indicator is scaled from 1 to 100 between that quarter's lowest and highest country and combined with the IRI weights.
cur.formula: score = 1 + 99 × (x − lowest) ÷ (highest − lowest), recalculated every quarter
cur.use: Good for ranking countries within one quarter. Not for tracking one country over time.
pros: Ranks countries well within one quarter
cons: A country's score moves when other countries move
About 1 in 5 yearly directions flips under small noise
Outlier caps give the same score to up to 33 countries

dyn.name: Dynamic min-max
dyn.tagline: The current IRI's idea without the outlier clipping.
dyn.how: Each quarter, every indicator is scaled from 0 to 100 between that quarter's lowest and highest country. There is no outlier treatment.
dyn.formula: score = 100 × (x − lowest) ÷ (highest − lowest), recalculated every quarter
dyn.use: A reference point: it shows what the moving ruler does without any clipping.
cons: Every other country moves when one country improves
One extreme value can set the whole scale

mdtf.name: Moving distance to frontier
mdtf.tagline: A fixed floor, but the top of the scale follows the best country.
mdtf.how: The floor is fixed (the trimmed 5th percentile of 2019 to 2024), but the frontier, which scores 100, resets every quarter to that quarter's best country.
mdtf.use: Shows why a fixed floor alone is not enough: a moving top still moves everyone.
pros: Part of the scale is fixed
cons: When the leader improves, everyone else falls further from 100
The largest cross-country effect of any method in random shocks

dea.name: Malmquist / DEA
dea.tagline: Each country is scored against the best performers, with its own best weights.
dea.how: Yearly efficiency on the four IRI pillars. Each country gets the weights that make it look best, and its score is how close it comes to the frontier of best-performing countries. Change over time is a Malmquist index. It works with yearly data, so quarters in the same year share one value.
dea.formula: efficiency = highest score the country can reach, with its own weights, without any country exceeding 100
dea.use: Answers "did this country improve, or did the leaders move?" but is hard to explain and ignores the IRI weights.
pros: Separates catching up from the frontier moving
cons: Ignores the IRI weights
Many countries tie on the frontier
Ranks shift by about 15 places on average
Other countries still move

pool.name: Pooled min-max
pool.tagline: One lowest and highest value for all years, then frozen.
pool.how: Every country's value from every quarter of 2019 to 2024 is pooled. The lowest and highest become the 0 and 100 marks, and they are then frozen.
pool.formula: score = 100 × (x − lowest in 2019 to 2024) ÷ (highest in 2019 to 2024 − lowest in 2019 to 2024)
pool.use: Works only if its reference values are never recomputed.
cons: Reference values come from a span of years, so revising that span moves everyone
Adding a new quarter to the window rewrites every earlier score

z.name: Base-year z-score
z.tagline: Measures each country against where the average country stood in 2019.
z.how: For each indicator, z is how many typical gaps (2019 standard deviations) a value sits from the 2019 average, flipped where lower is better. The z values are combined with the IRI weights and shown as 50 + 10z. A fixed cap of 3 to 5 stops any one indicator dominating.
z.formula: z = (x − 2019 average) ÷ 2019 standard deviation;  shown as 50 + 10 × z
z.use: The IRI's main method for tracking progress and comparing countries.
cons: The scale has no fixed limits, so it needs a fixed cap
Changing the base year needs a new method version
z.usedBy: Similar to the base-year standardisation used by the Corruption Perceptions Index

dtf.name: Distance to frontier
dtf.tagline: How far a country is from the best value ever recorded.
dtf.how: The frontier (100) is the best value recorded in 2019 to 2024, and the floor (0) is the trimmed 5th percentile. Both are frozen and scores are capped between 0 and 100.
dtf.formula: score = 100 × (x − floor) ÷ (frontier − floor), capped at 0 and 100
dtf.use: Works only if its reference values are never recomputed. Beyond the frontier, gains are not credited.
pros: Simple message: percent of the way to the best
cons: Reference values come from a span of years
A new record is never credited, because the top is 100
Ties countries at the bottom on several indicators
dtf.usedBy: The idea behind the World Bank's Doing Business distance to frontier

fg.name: Fixed goalposts
fg.tagline: A preset floor and target for every indicator.
fg.how: Each indicator has a floor (0) and a target (100) chosen in advance: natural bounds where they exist, otherwise the 2019 to 2024 record plus 10 percent headroom. Scores are capped between 0 and 100.
fg.formula: score = 100 × (x − floor) ÷ (target − floor), capped at 0 and 100
fg.use: The alternative if ISOC needs a bounded 0 to 100 scale.
cons: 27 sets of targets to agree and defend
Gains stop counting at the target
Where goalposts are set too low, up to 24 countries tie
fg.usedBy: The approach of the UNDP Human Development Index

dtt.name: Distance to target
dtt.tagline: How far a country is from an ambitious policy target.
dtt.how: Each indicator has a floor (the worst value recorded) and an ambitious target: the 90th percentile pushed a further 50 percent beyond. Scores are capped between 0 and 100.
dtt.formula: score = 100 × (x − floor) ÷ (target − floor), capped at 0 and 100
dtt.use: A useful extra view of progress toward goals, not the main score.
pros: Speaks the language of policy targets
cons: Less stable year to year
Progress stops counting at the target
Targets must be chosen and defended

ampi.name: AMPI
ampi.tagline: Rewards balanced progress and penalises uneven profiles.
ampi.how: Indicators are rescaled so 100 is the 2019 average, then the score is the average M minus a penalty S²/M for how uneven the 27 indicators are. All indicators count equally.
ampi.formula: AMPI = M − S² ÷ M, where M and S are the mean and spread of a country's 27 rescaled indicators
ampi.use: An extra view of how balanced a country's progress is.
pros: Shows whether progress is broad or lopsided
cons: Ignores the IRI weights
The penalty can lower the score of a strong performer
Not fully independent of other countries in Test 1
